scenes.tts: Something has to clear the potassium from the space outside neurons. Who does it, and how?
scenes.visual: The neuron and its narrow extracellular space from chapter 1, with K+ dots crowded outside. The question appears above.
scenes.narration: Something has to clear the potassium from the space outside neurons. Who does it, and how?

scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-six, Stephen Kuffler, John Nicholls and Richard Orkand recorded from glial cells.
scenes.caption: In 1966, Stephen Kuffler, John Nicholls and Richard Orkand recorded from glial cells.
scenes.visual: Title card: Orkand, Nicholls and Kuffler, 1966.
scenes.narration: In 1966, Stephen Kuffler, John Nicholls and Richard Orkand recorded from glial cells.

scenes.tts: They worked in the optic nerve of an amphibian, the mudpuppy.
scenes.caption: They worked in the optic nerve of an amphibian, the mudpuppy Necturus.
scenes.visual: A schematic optic nerve of Necturus, the mudpuppy: axons with a glial cell between them, a microelectrode in the glial cell.
scenes.narration: They worked in the optic nerve of an amphibian, the mudpuppy Necturus.

scenes.tts: Read the record first. The glial cell's voltage sits steady and very negative.
scenes.visual: A glial voltage trace drawn flat and low on the screen, with a row of axon spikes above it (none yet).
scenes.narration: Read the record first. The glial cell's voltage sits steady and very negative.

scenes.tts: Then the neighbouring axons fire a train of impulses. The glial cell slowly depolarizes.
scenes.visual: A row of axon spikes appears above; beneath it the glial trace slowly rises during the train.
scenes.narration: Then the neighbouring axons fire a train of impulses. The glial cell slowly depolarizes.

scenes.tts: Longer and faster trains depolarize it more. When the axons stop, it recovers over seconds.
scenes.visual: Two more trains, one longer and one faster, give bigger glial depolarizations. After each train the trace returns slowly; a time bar reads seconds.
scenes.narration: Longer and faster trains depolarize it more. When the axons stop, it recovers over seconds.

scenes.tts: What is the glial cell sensing?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. What is the glial cell sensing?
scenes.narration: What is the glial cell sensing?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Potassium. Changing the potassium in the bath moved the glial voltage as a potassium electrode's would.
scenes.visual: The bath around the nerve changes shade as its K+ is raised; the glial trace steps up with each change. Label: behaves like a potassium electrode.
scenes.narration: Potassium. Changing the potassium in the bath moved the glial voltage as a potassium electrode's would.

scenes.tts: So the glia were sensing the potassium the axons released as it built up.
scenes.visual: K+ dots leave the firing axons and crowd around the glial cell; the glial trace rises with them.
scenes.narration: So the glia were sensing the potassium the axons released as it built up.

scenes.tts: Astrocytes are joined by gap junctions, channels that link the insides of neighbouring cells. Their membranes are almost purely permeable to potassium.
scenes.visual: An astrocyte network: several astrocytes joined by small gap-junction dots. Label: membranes almost purely permeable to K+.
scenes.narration: Astrocytes are joined by gap junctions, channels that link the insides of neighbouring cells. Their membranes are almost purely permeable to potassium.

scenes.tts: In this simplified, strongly coupled network, the astrocytes stay at nearly the same voltage. What differs from place to place is the local E K, set by the local potassium.
scenes.caption: In this simplified, strongly coupled network, the astrocytes stay at nearly the same voltage. What differs from place to place is the local E_K, set by the local potassium.
scenes.visual: One nearly shared voltage line runs through the whole network, near E_K, drawn as a schematic approximation. At each site a small local E_K tick sits at a slightly different height. On screen: nearly shared voltage, a strong-coupling approximation; local E_K depends on local potassium.
scenes.narration: In this simplified, strongly coupled network, the astrocytes stay at nearly the same voltage. What differs from place to place is the local E_K, set by the local potassium.

scenes.tts: Now let one spot fire hard. There, the local E K is more positive than the network's voltage.
scenes.caption: Now let one spot fire hard. There, the local E_K is more positive than the network's voltage.
scenes.visual: Three sites along the network, each with the same small voltage scale. At site one, K+ is high and its local E_K tick sits above the network's voltage line.
scenes.narration: Now let one spot fire hard. There, the local E_K is more positive than the network's voltage.

scenes.tts: So potassium flows in. In this model it enters through the potassium channel Kir four point one.
scenes.caption: So potassium flows in. In this model it enters through the potassium channel Kir4.1.
scenes.visual: Arrows point into the astrocyte at site one, through channels labelled Kir4.1.
scenes.narration: So potassium flows in. In this model it enters through the potassium channel Kir4.1.

scenes.tts: That entry depolarizes the network slightly. Where potassium is still low, potassium now flows out.
scenes.visual: The network's voltage line nudges up. At sites two and three, the local E_K ticks now sit below it, and arrows point out.
scenes.narration: That entry depolarizes the network slightly. Where potassium is still low, potassium now flows out.

scenes.tts: Entry and exit happen at the same time, as one loop of current. This is spatial buffering.
scenes.visual: Both sets of arrows appear at the same instant, joined by a closed current loop through the network. Label: spatial buffering. Note: potassium can leave far away without waiting for the ions that entered to travel there.
scenes.narration: Entry and exit happen at the same time, as one loop of current. This is spatial buffering.

scenes.tts: It moves potassium from where it is high to where it is low. On balance, the potassium stays outside, only spread thinner.
scenes.visual: Arrows in at site one and out at sites two and three; the crowd of K+ dots at site one thins while dots spread along the network. Label: Redistribution: in here, out there; on balance still outside, spread thinner.
scenes.narration: It moves potassium from where it is high to where it is low. On balance, the potassium stays outside, only spread thinner.

scenes.tts: Putting it back inside cells is a separate job. Sodium-potassium pumps in astrocytes and neurons take potassium up.
scenes.visual: A pump icon on an astrocyte and another on a neuron move K+ dots inward. Label: Uptake: back inside.
scenes.narration: Putting it back inside cells is a separate job. Sodium-potassium pumps in astrocytes and neurons take potassium up.

scenes.tts: How much each mechanism contributes is still debated.
scenes.visual: The two labels side by side, Redistribution and Uptake, with a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: How much each mechanism contributes is still debated.

scenes.tts: Ken McCarthy's laboratory deleted Kir four point one from glia in mice.
scenes.caption: Ken McCarthy's laboratory deleted Kir4.1 from glia in mice.
scenes.visual: A mouse icon and an astrocyte with its Kir4.1 channels crossed out. Label: glial Kir4.1 knockout.
scenes.narration: Ken McCarthy's laboratory deleted Kir4.1 from glia in mice.

scenes.tts: In hippocampal slices, astrocytes lacking the channel took up potassium poorly.
scenes.visual: An astrocyte potassium-uptake trace: control large, knockout small. Label: CA1 astrocytes, slices from mice 15 to 20 days old.
scenes.narration: In hippocampal slices, astrocytes lacking the channel took up potassium poorly.

scenes.tts: What else might fail when this potassium channel is gone?
scenes.visual: A question mark hovers over a glutamate transporter on the astrocyte. On screen: Pause. What else might fail?
scenes.narration: What else might fail when this potassium channel is gone?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Glutamate uptake. That does not mean the channel carries glutamate. Glutamate transport depends on the astrocyte's voltage.
scenes.visual: The glutamate-uptake trace: control large, knockout small. A voltage meter on the astrocyte drifts up from negative.
scenes.narration: Glutamate uptake. That does not mean the channel carries glutamate. Glutamate transport depends on the astrocyte's voltage.

scenes.tts: And Kir four point one helps hold that voltage negative.
scenes.caption: And Kir4.1 helps hold that voltage negative.
scenes.visual: The Kir4.1 channels return and the voltage meter drops back to negative.
scenes.narration: And Kir4.1 helps hold that voltage negative.

scenes.tts: One limit. The deletion began in development, and it also reached oligodendrocytes.
scenes.visual: A timeline marks the deletion starting early in development; an oligodendrocyte beside the astrocyte also shows a crossed-out channel.
scenes.narration: One limit. The deletion began in development, and it also reached oligodendrocytes.

scenes.tts: So the result cannot be pinned on mature astrocytes alone.
scenes.visual: Label: cannot be pinned on mature astrocytes alone.
scenes.narration: So the result cannot be pinned on mature astrocytes alone.

scenes.tts: So astrocytes sense the potassium that firing releases. They spread it through their network, and pumps take it back inside cells.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: astrocytes sense released K+; spatial buffering spreads it through the network; pumps in astrocytes and neurons take it back inside.
scenes.narration: So astrocytes sense the potassium that firing releases. They spread it through their network, and pumps take it back inside cells.
